<note>The image described in the transcription is a classic "memento mori" portrait. By placing a human skull next to mathematical tools like the compass and ruler, the artist reminds the viewer that while human knowledge and science are grand, life is fleeting. The smoke and flames rising from the skull symbolize the soul or the transitory nature of worldly existence.</note>

<note>original Latin: "CAROLO Francorum Regi Christianissimo & inuictissimo, Gabriel Collangelius Aluernas Turonicus fœlicitatem." This is a standard formal greeting to the monarch, Charles IX, who had recently ascended the throne.</note>

The printers had not yet, or rather had not spent even the slightest amount of time and effort on publishing this present *Polygraphy* <note>original: "Polygraphiæ". This refers to the work on cryptography and secret writing by Johannes Trithemius, which Collange translated into French and expanded with his own systems.</note>, Most Christian King of the French Charles <note>Charles IX was only ten years old when he became king in 1560.</note>, when the dread iniquity of the fates snatched from us King Francis <note>Francis II, the elder brother of Charles IX, who died unexpectedly in December 1560 after only seventeen months on the throne.</note> your brother, not without the heavy grief and sorrow of his people. --- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to King Charles IX. The translator, Gabriel de Collange, describes his despair following the sudden death of King Francis II, which threatened the publication of his work, and how noble scholars encouraged him to continue the project in honor of the new young king.</meta>

you, not only were holidays <note>original: "feriae". Work stopped on the printing press due to the period of mourning for King Francis II.</note> proclaimed for the **printers**, but indeed, every hope of the favor—which my mind was confident I would obtain from the prince—was snatched away, delaying my study and my labor. For what did the sudden fall of the Prince bring to wretched me, either to hope well for a beneficial return (with which kings are accustomed to receive the works of scholars), or at least to not risk the expenses, which I had certainly already begun then, and now persevere in making as large as possible, in bringing the light to this work? 

This one thing kept recurring to my mind: that soon there would be a loss to my affairs, which no subsequent labor, however great, and no vigils <note>original: "vigiliae". Refers to the "burning of the midnight oil" or late-night scholarly work.</note>, however heavy and sleepless, could repair. And so I was anxiously struggling, and as if without hope, I was revoking the plan I had previously intended concerning the publication of the <term>Polygraphy: A method of secret writing or cryptography, from the Greek 'poly' (many) and 'graphia' (writing)</term>, when I was summoned voluntarily by many, whose learning is not at all to be regretted; indeed, if their learning were compared with their ancestral nobility, it is uncertain which of the two would yield to the other. 

In order to add a swifter stimulus to me—just as they were intensely eager for the *Polygraphy* (which I had entirely decided to suppress) to be released into the public—so, by acting precisely as <term>Panegyrists: Orators who deliver speeches of high praise, typically for a monarch</term> of the virtues which raise you above the other princes of the **Christian world**, they celebrated so many of your...

...praises of your name, so that they seemed to affirm to me that there is no one—I will not say in dignity (since no one similar to you can be found anywhere)—but even in age, who is not only your equal but even much older, for whom the "lamp" <note>original: "lucerna". This refers to the metaphorical "smell of the lamp," a classical idiom signifying the diligent nighttime study and labor of scholars.</note> of the most learned men would smell more sweetly. 

Furthermore, all the nobles of your kingdom added that, because of your character—as brilliant as it is royal—they have constantly persuaded themselves of this one thing: that our **France** <note>original: "Galliæ"</note> will not lack its own **Augustus**, **Trajan**, **Probus**, **Constantine**, **Charlemagne**, or indeed, its own **Charles of Valois** <note>The King Charles IX (1550–1574), of the House of Valois, to whom this work is dedicated.</note>, if the fates preserve you safe and sound for a long time (which we all strive for with a solemn vow to the Powers above). They believe you are a ruler who, through integrity of character, pure justice, generosity, and skill in both letters and arms, might not only equal these most powerful governors of the Roman Empire, but might even surpass and outmeasure their glorious fame through a longer sequence of great deeds. 

This **praising commemoration** <note>original: "encomiastica... commemoratio"</note> of you by such celebrated men, O most illustrious King, first stirred **Collange** <note>The author, Gabriel de Collange (c. 1524–1572), refers to himself here by the Latinized version of his name, "Collangelium".</note>, who was then sluggish with inactivity. It moved him to contemplate the innate gifts of your mind—gifts which, once they have matured, will advance toward the strength and summit of the most absolute virtue. It also moved him to weigh more closely the greatness of the Empire which you hold by inheritance and which you acknowledge as received from Heaven alone. After these matters were more diligently weighed, finally a reason—

...it was prophesied <note>The text begins mid-word with "-cinaretur," likely completing "vaticinaretur" from the previous page.</note> that there is no other prince in whose name and under whose favorable divine protection the **Polygraphia** <term>Polygraphia: The title of this work, meaning "many ways of writing." Then, by running through even the smallest part of it with a quick reading, they might instill my name into your ears, so that I might feel I have not entirely wasted my labor and my **oil** <note>original: "oleũ" (oleum). IT IS AN ANCIENT opinion <note>original: "Vetus est opinio."</note>, repeated almost from the very first men, O most Christian King of the French <note>original: "Francorum Rex Christianissime." This was a traditional title for the Kings of France, emphasizing their role as defenders of the Church.</note>, that among all things which are most dear to each of us in their own right, the Commonwealth <term>Commonwealth: From the Latin "Respublica," meaning the state, the public interest, or the "common weal," rather than a specific political system.</term> stands so supreme in that regard that there is no one who would not willingly undertake all things for the sake of preserving and increasing it. <meta>This page continues the dedication to King Francis. The previous page established the importance of the Commonwealth (the state) over private interests. The author, Gabriel de Collange, now explains his personal contribution to the defense and prosperity of France.</meta>

...as if things to be consecrated: for the one Commonwealth has far surpassed all the affections of all people. And so, when I saw in this most happy age of your reign very many people, busying themselves with French affairs, applying themselves eagerly to their tasks: this man making Italian <term>Pyrotechnia: Literally "fire-art," referring here to the technical skills of metallurgy and military engineering—such as gunpowder and cannons—which were being adapted from Italian manuals into French.</term> French, that man devising an incredible method for fortifying and besieging cities, another deserving well of the Commonwealth through unheard-of stratagems and new inventions: lest I alone should seem an idler among so many people most intent on their work, I thought I would do something worthwhile if I were to roll my tub <note>original: "dolium meum vltro citróque versarem." This is a famous anecdote about the philosopher Diogenes. While the citizens of Corinth were frantically preparing for a siege, Diogenes, having nothing else to do, rolled his ceramic tub back and forth so he wouldn't be the only one not "busy."</note> back and forth, imitating <term>Diogenes: A Greek Cynic philosopher famous for his minimalist lifestyle and his sharp critiques of social vanity.</term>: and, according to the modest measure of my literary ability, I might bring some gift into your Commonwealth (as if into a common <term>gazophylacium: A word derived from Greek and Persian meaning a treasury or storehouse, often used in the Bible to refer to the temple treasury.</term> treasury).

Since, however, kings and princes cannot manage everything by themselves, and in those matters where they cannot be present personally, the delegated loyalty of friends and allies is substituted for their own efforts—those whom, being far away, they cannot inform by common letters without great danger. This is especially true in these times where, with a prevailing license for sinning and loyalty seemingly put to sleep, even the letters of Kings sealed with the royal ring are not spared by the interceptors of mail and the vultures <note>original: "vultures." Collange uses this harsh metaphor to describe spies and corrupt officials who "scavenge" for secrets in intercepted state correspondence.</note> of the more secret council of the kingdom: I reckoned it would be most beneficial to French affairs if the [work] of John

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to the King of France (likely Charles IX or Henry III, given the references to Francis and Henry as grandfather and father). It completes the sentence from the previous page, which warned that if such works were not published, they would be left to rot or remain "unborn."</meta>

...would feed the moths, and like premature and poorly conceived offspring, they would lack the blessing of Lucina <term>Lucina: The Roman goddess of childbirth, responsible for bringing the fetus safely into the light.</term>. Whichever of these might happen, I will not cease to entreat your Majesty with humble prayers (although I am now striving to do this at greater length) that you might receive my devotion in this matter with no other spirit than that which makes you a King: for your great inclination toward those who seek to illuminate your Republic with literary monuments is already spoken of and proclaimed among foreign nations. 

Moreover, the examples of ancient kings lead me to firmly believe that you will not turn away. If such examples carry any weight with you, then those of Francis and Henry—your grandfather and father—do so most of all. The latter [Henry], as he died, left behind his kingdom, crown, scepter, humanity, and his zeal and love for peace. The former [Francis] gave you his hereditary name at the heavenly washing of the sacred fonts <note>original: "cœleſti ſacrorum fontium lauachro," a poetic reference to the King's baptism.</note>, along with such a great inclination toward letters and all learned men, that you are destined to receive no less glory than your grandfather (who was heard of so magnificently even among the barbarians for his reputation in letters). 

Since you model and adorn yourself entirely after the characters of those princes, I do not expect my labor to be in vain for you. Rather, I expect you will receive my sleepless efforts as favorably as the Emperor Augustus received the *Architecture* of **Vitruvius**, or as **Deiotarius**, the Tetrarch of Galatia, received the work on agriculture offered to him by **Diophanes**...

# GABRIEL COLLANGELIUS, of Auvergne and Tours,
## To the Reader.
### CONCERNING THE KABBALAH <note>Gabriel de Collange (c. 1524–1572) uses the term "Cabala" here to refer to the study of hidden or mystical knowledge, which he sought to reconcile with Renaissance science.</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring elaborate foliage and vine scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

INDEED, the characters of men are so disposed—especially in these times—that there is nowhere a more hostile enemy of literature, nor one who hates the noble arts more fundamentally, than he who is shrouded in the thick darkness of ignorance. Being devoid of all knowledge himself, he cannot bear for the brilliant works of others to enjoy their rightful praise; instead, he disparages them with his words and strikes them down with contempt.

This has now become so common among all people that it seems nature herself has planted this trait within us. It is as if we were made for no other purpose than to be impatient with the truth, detesting it as if with cursed proclamations, or attributing to an evil genius <note>original: "malo genio," a classical reference to a malevolent spirit or bad luck used to explain away extraordinary achievements</note> those things which have come into the light only through the singular blessing of the immortal Gods <note>original: "Deorum immortalium," a standard Renaissance Latin phrasing for the Divine, despite the author being a Christian monk</note>. These are truths that have left men of a certain sluggish leisure <term>supine leisure: from "supini cuiusdam otij," referring to an inactive or lazy state of mind that is easily shocked by profound or new learning</term> with no small sense of wonder. Thus it was with the self-restraint of John the Baptist...

<summary>In this preface, Gabriel de Collange laments the intellectual climate of his time, criticizing ignorant people who reflexively hate or dismiss profound scholarly discoveries. He argues that new truths are often suppressed by the lazy or the jealous rather than being recognized as divine gifts.</summary>
<keywords>Gabriel de Collange, Kabbalah, ignorance, intellectual jealousy, human nature, John the Baptist, Renaissance scholarship, hidden truth</keywords>

To recall these, as if by the right of restoration <term>postliminy: from "post-liminio," a Roman legal term for the recovery of rights by a person returning from captivity</term>, and to put them to some practical use, is the mark of a man serving not his own interests, but the benefit of the Commonwealth. 

Among these disciplines, however, there is no one who does not grieve that the Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabalam Hebræorum," referring to Jewish mystical and oral tradition</note> of the Hebrews—an art as ancient as it is most truthful—lies neglected and covered in the grime of dust. This is especially true because the wisest of the Hebrews maintain with unwavering conviction that it was handed down by God, the Best and Greatest, to Moses. They assert that it was communicated to the wise (though not to just anyone, but to those deemed fit), and thereafter entrusted to posterity through certain degrees of succession without written records <note>original: "citra literarū monumenta," meaning without the use of books or permanent writing</note>, solely by the service of the living voice, until the time of Ezra. 

Not foreign to this practice of the Jews is the ancient institution of Lysis and Archippus <note>Two famous disciples of Pythagoras who were said to have survived the persecution of the sect</note>, who, while teaching the discipline of Pythagoras at Thebes, commanded their disciples to use their intellect and memory, [rather than] books...

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the Kabbalah's origins, specifically how it was passed down through oral tradition rather than written texts. It addresses the ignorance of critics who misunderstand the nature of this wisdom.</meta>

...es in place of books. And so, this art received the name of **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabalae," from the Hebrew 'qabbalah', meaning 'received tradition'</note>, a word which signifies and implies "reception" to us. It is so named because it was received by hearing alone, and was preserved intact without the use of letters <margin>Cælius Rhodiginus, Book 10, chapter 1. <note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1450–1525), a scholar known as Cælius Rhodiginus, who wrote the 'Antiquae Lectiones'.</note></margin>. 

If we accept this as most certain—as reason surely suggests—there is no reason for us to be moved by the staggering recklessness and arrogance of certain people. In order to bark at things that are by their very nature beautiful and pure, and to earn some reputation through slander (since they cannot do so through virtue or duty), these people betray their own impudence to such an extent that they assert **Kabbalah** was once a man condemned for heresy, and they proclaim all "Kabbalists" to be heretics. 

Such vile little men are born with stubborn minds and a hatred for good literature; to them, nothing tastes good unless it is tasteless. Nothing seems learned to them unless it is so common and exposed to the common rabble—that great teacher of error—that it is known even to the bleary-eyed and to barbers <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus," a classical idiom from the Roman poet Horace, referring to news or gossip so common that everyone at the local barbershop knows it</note>. 

However, if something is locked away behind the bolts of hidden mysteries, and does not allow unrefined and unlearned minds even the slightest knowledge of itself, it is immediately—in their judgment—either erroneous or distributed to men who have been seduced (as they say) by the art and service of evil demons, following secret arts too superstitiously. There is no one who cannot easily see with what hisses such an opinion should be driven off...

To this discipline, the Hebrew **Merkavah** <term>Merkavah: From the Hebrew for "chariot," this refers to a branch of Jewish mysticism centered on the vision of God's throne-chariot in the Book of Ezekiel.</term> is not merely similar, but deeply related. One would not be foolish to judge that both were given by the immortal Gods, and that they have no commerce with spirits or demons; rather, both contribute greatly to divine worship, the salvation of humanity, and the understanding of truth. This is a fact that the very nature of the subject can surely demonstrate, even to those who, out of a sheer desire for contradiction, might wish to rise up against this art.

## Apology.

**P**many maintain and are of the opinion that all the ancient **Philosophers** and learned personages have, with all their power, sought the means and industry to record and put into **hidden** and **covered writing** <note>This refers to cryptography and esoteric writing intended to protect knowledge.</note>, everything that through their assiduous labor and extreme diligence they were able to discover in the **secrets of nature**: so that, by this means, these things might not be understood, and even less known, by the wicked and malicious, who (following their evil habits) might or would want to abuse them. # PROLOGUE TO
->all of Polygraphy.<- <note>The term "Polygraphy" (from the Greek for "many writings") refers to the art of cryptography and the various methods of hiding a message within different forms of text.</note>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'N' at the beginning of the text, intricately decorated with foliate patterns and scrolling vines inside a square border.</image-desc>

WE READ that several ancient learned philosophers, kings, princes, lords, and other great personages long ago invented diverse and variable means by which they could safely entrust their secrets and counsels to messengers sent by them (however far away it might be). This was done so that, along the way, they might be rendered immune and exempt from the pursuit and searching of observers; so that the simplicity of the Cabalists <note>The author likely refers to those who search for hidden or mystical meanings, similar to practitioners of Kabbalah.</note> would not uncover the mystery, and so that the natural curiosity of the Baccuceans <note>original: "Baccucées". ### ON THE CONTENTS OF THE SECOND BOOK OF POLYGRAPHY.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'A' at the beginning of the text, featuring a Roman-style character within a square frame filled with intricate, symmetrical floral and vine patterns on a dark, hatched background.</image-desc>

**In the second book** of Polygraphy, I have, not without good counsel and reason, transcended the ends and limits of all natural language, by adopting a strange, new, and foreign one: desiring by this means, in imitation of the barbarians, to wander further afield. For through these mythological paraphrases <note>The author uses "paraphrases" to describe the cover-text—innocent-looking words or stories that hide a secret meaning.</note> contained in this book, and arranged in good order, I show a path very easy and simple to reach the **artificial unity**, through which at all times, one can communicate to one’s **binary** <note>In this context, the "unity" refers to the sender or the single source of the code, while the "binary" refers to the recipient or the second person in the communication chain.</note> symbolic notes and understandings most securely and secretly.

And if in this, your <term>philologue</term> <note>Literally a "lover of words" or a linguist; here referring to the person attempting to decode the text.</note> is not prudently advised, he will render the binary totally contrary to the **monad** <note>The monad represents the "One" or the original state of the message; the author is using Pythagorean mathematical terms to describe the relationship between the hidden message and its interpretation.</note>: inasmuch as the single **ternary**, proceeding from the unity and also from the binary, like a **palindrome** <note>original: "palydrome"; something that runs back and forth or is the same in both directions.</note>, contains and encompasses within itself both the one and the other: so that, if the utility of necessary reason is extended beyond the limits of the matter and subject proposed: one must count and calculate the paraphrases from the beginning of the day until the <term>minutes</term> create and constitute the degree at which night is made equal to day. <note>An astronomical metaphor for finding the "equilibrium" or the exact setting required to sync the cipher.</note> 

The manner of this secret image maintains within itself a good and perpetual silence, fearing not at all the frauds and deceptions of the <term>Baccuceans</term> <note>A term for prying eyes or "gaping" fools who try to spy on secrets.</note> or others. And it can be extended into as great an abundance as you wish. And it can also be changed and varied by infinite and innumerable means, as much by **orchemes** <note>Derived from the Greek word for dance or rhythmic movement; likely referring to the rhythmic arrangement of words in the code.</note> as by **metatheses**. <note>The transposition or rearrangement of letters or units within the cipher.</note>

### ON THE CONTENTS OF THE THIRD BOOK

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' within a rectangular woodcut frame featuring floral vines and foliate patterns, with a stylized face or cherub visible in the bottom-left corner.</image-desc>**In the third book** of Polygraphy, we may have great confidence in the **binary** <note>The "binary" refers to the second person in the communication chain—the receiver of the secret message.</note>, by which, all obstacles ceasing and without difficulty, we can return and be reduced to **unity** <note>The "unity" refers to the sender or the singular source/key of the code.</note>, even from the first and only glance. # TREATISE ON THE FIFTH
## BOOK OF POLYGRAPHY

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A'. The letter is constructed with foliate and architectural motifs. It is flanked by two nude figures standing on scrolls. At the top of the initial block is a stylized leaf or fleur-de-lis motif. The background of the letter block features horizontal and vertical cross-hatching.</image-desc>

**Having**, through this fifth and final book of Polygraphy, introduced and expressed in proper order the spiritual and mental narration of nearly all the preceding mysteries and secrets—by degrees and signs, and also by arithmetic distributions—I have acquired the functions and understandings of the <term>grammates</term> <note>original: "grammates." From the Greek for 'letters'; here referring to the use of letters as numerical signs.</note> and characters through the proper administration of the Kabbalistic <note>Refers to the Jewish mystical tradition of interpreting secret meanings in texts, which Renaissance scholars like Trithemius adapted for cryptography.</note> operation. One may further find a certain mystery hidden and occult within the shell and the husk <note>A metaphor for the literal text (the husk) concealing the secret meaning (the kernel or mystery).</note>, and another totally different mystery will be found and known in the common operation of the signs. For just as the spirit together with the blood gives life to the human body, no more and no less does the latent power in this art command and hold the operation within itself. Therefore, he for whom the invention of this art may be necessary must open the eyes of the mind, so that he may easily understand the specific property of each one's operation. I would desire that the whole might be as well known and understood by the good and the just, as I wish it never to be manifested, known, or understood by the wicked and the reprobate. THE END OF this first book of <term>Polygraphy</term> <note>From the Greek 'polys' (many) and 'graphein' (to write); the art of secret writing through various methods.</note> gives me great pleasure and satisfaction: for having acquired through it a more ample speed and assurance, I am determined to test the strength and capacity of my spirit in the description of the remaining books. This will be no less a labor than a contemplation: inasmuch as every newly discovered <term>science</term> <note>In the 16th century, 'science' referred more broadly to a system of knowledge or a specialized skill.</note>, at its beginning, troubles the one who is its inventor—seeing himself followed by everyone, yet having no one who precedes him. Nevertheless, it is certain that every beginning, however difficult it may be, once practiced and understood through some use, gives the author and inventor greater assurance and boldness. 

This (I think) will be granted to me in finishing (with God’s help) this first book of Polygraphy: which I have totally distinguished and separated into three hundred seventy-six <term>minutiae</term> <note>original: "minuties"; here referring to the individual cipher tables or small components of the code.</note> or alphabets, placing before each of them (as you can see) the proper degrees of <term>paraphrasms</term> <note>original: "paraphrasmes"; these are the specific phrases used to hide the secret letters. In this system, writing a series of pious phrases actually spells out a hidden message.</note>, so that, when you have arranged and set the whole in good order, you will find a sufficiently good prayer, and Christian and Catholic exhortation, contained and comprised in and by nine thousand twenty-four phrases or paraphrasms, well and duly ordered and joined in every way and everywhere. 

And nothing will be lacking or missing for all studious people who take the trouble to understand this science; they shall have the means, mode, method, perfect power, and faculty to write and announce to one another surely and secretly, and without suspicion, however far they may be removed from all mystical and secret affairs. All things comprised and contained in the circle or circuit of this art and science, proceeding from the point and period, of which the <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "athomes"; used here metaphorically to mean the most basic, indivisible parts of the system.</note> and minutiae are and...

## of Polygraphy.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap letter 'P' decorated with interlacing vines and acanthus leaves.</image-desc>

Since the beginning, creation, and <term>exordium</term> <note>original: "exorde"; the formal beginning or introduction of something, often used in rhetoric.</note> of the world, the division and difference of bodies and persons, along with the variety of minds and wills, have confounded the unity and singularity of tongues and languages; following what is truly said and witnessed by the Holy Gospel, saying, "From the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" <note>original: "De l'abondance du cueur la bouche parle"; a translation of the Latin Vulgate, Matthew 12:34: *Ex abundantia enim cordis os loquitur*.</note> with the tongue, which is the instrument and sole means of providing understanding and knowledge of what the mind has thought or is thinking internally. And as for the understanding of the secrets of the mind reduced to sense and knowledge, there are many and infinite means, the nature of which can be changed by usage, and also by art. Usage, established and introduced by whim, is common and known to many, and by many; but art and science are known and understood by very few people. It is certain that it would be difficult, indeed impossible, to state and record in writing in how many ways and manners (within the last six or eight hundred years) the unregulated languages—of the French, Italians, Spaniards, as well as Germans, and universally of other nations—have been changed and varied. The sea comes and goes, flows and ebbs. But once man has expired,

<summary>Trithemius opens Book Two by reflecting on how human diversity and the "abundance of the heart" led to the variety of world languages. He distinguishes between common "usage" of language and the specialized "art" of secret communication known only to a few.</summary>

purpose, I have not without good reason placed and described this second book of Polygraphy after the first: considering that just as there is diversity and variety in human wills (as has been said), for this reason one provides, or ought to provide, several and variable means, serving good and honest operations. In the first and preceding book, the day shines and gives light to the night; but in this one, and the other following books, the day has no light, nor does it receive any. In the first, light leads the shadow into light: but in this one, the blind man enlightens and illuminates the blind, and without eyes gives and administers to the darkness the clarity and the sight that it does not have. In this one, the night covers and envelops the day in perpetual obscurity. And one going and walking in the darkness (without light) can easily lead and guide the blind. <note>This table provides three distinct "alphabets" for substitution. In column 1, the words are built on the root "lazar-" (reminiscent of the biblical Lazarus). Column 2 uses "styom-" (a pseudo-Greek construction). Column 3 uses a mix of "aft-" and "st-" roots. To encode a message, a user would select one word from a column to represent a specific letter. By rotating through these columns, the user ensures that the same letter in the original message is represented by a different word each time, a method known as a polyalphabetic cipher.</note>

By using a different column for each successive letter, the author ensures that the same letter in the original message is never represented by the same word twice in a row, a technique intended to baffle anyone attempting to break the code.</note>

<note>
This page presents another segment of the "clavis" or key. In this system, each letter of the alphabet is represented by a specific invented word. The words are categorized into columns (1, 2, and 3). To encrypt a message, the user would cycle through these columns: the first letter of the secret message is swapped for a word in Column 1, the second letter for a word in Column 2, and so on. This creates a "polyalphabetic" cipher, making it much harder to crack than a simple one-for-one substitution.
</note>

### BOOK TWO

<note>
This table serves as a "lexicon" of invented words used for encryption. In this polyalphabetic system, a scribe would not simply replace one letter with another, but would replace a letter with an entire word. By moving from column 1 to 2 to 3 for each successive letter of a secret message, the resulting text would look like a string of nonsensical or foreign vocabulary, masking the true contents. The numbers 697–720 provide a unique index for every word in the third column of the series.
</note>

By cycling through columns—using column 1 for the first letter, column 2 for the second, and so on—the sender ensures that the same letter in the original message is represented by different words in the ciphertext, making it much harder for a codebreaker to recognize patterns.</note>

# SECOND BOOK

Following the promise made at the beginning and introduction of this second book of Polygraphy, presently finished, it seems to me that, by the triple number of alphabets contained therein, I have duly and sufficiently satisfied the reader by example and similarity; so that one might have and find, by means of these, a new form, mode, manner, and phrase for writing very securely and secretly. In and by this book, I conduct and lead the "night"—which serves for sure secrecy—through the shadow and obscurity of the paraphrases or the number contained in the said four lines, including the numerical lines that make up the fourth. There are 1,176 minute parts <term>minutiae: the individual vocabulary entries or "roots" in the cipher tables</term>, having their own fixed and stable degrees, which you can easily expand through an infinity of instances and phrases. These will serve to hide and cover all secrets you wish to write, in all countries and nations, and in all languages and places in the world. And whenever the night <note>Metaphor for the encrypted text.</note> passes, or shall pass, the image and line of day <note>Metaphor for the plain text.</note>, you may easily (whenever you wish and when it is necessary) bring back the small circle <term>orbicule: a circular diagram or "volvelle" used to align cipher alphabets</term> and the linear ring coming from the point, to the path and way by which you came. And if much of the night remained to be written, bring back, if you see fit, the tail of the dragon to the head and beginning <note>Original: "la queue du dragon au chef." An astronomical metaphor (the lunar nodes) used here to describe resetting the cipher sequence to the start.</note>. But above all, it is necessary and must be noted that your partner <term>binaire: the person intended to receive and decode the message</term> and kabbalistic recipient duly knows and understands your notes and lines of unity. Now, he who is greatly hungry must work greatly, so that by means of his diligent and great work and toil, he may have food to eat. Yet it seems to me that there is no need for great labor or toil to lead and direct this where you wish. It makes a sufficiently large progression of its own accord and advances by itself.

ON POLYGRAPHY.
x ij

# EPILOGUE AND END OF THE
## third book of Polygraphy.

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'A' decorated with intricate floral patterns and scrolling foliage within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
Having duly described and explained previously, through sound and certain demonstration and experience, the nature, power, and understanding of this new invention: I do not intend to make a longer discourse here, considering that the path, or experiments <note>In this context, "experiments" refers to practical applications or demonstrations of the cipher system.</note>, described in this third book, can provide infinite and innumerable means to any practitioner who has, or might have, need of a more ample and extensive model. I also think it unnecessary here to recount or bring back to memory what was previously said and written in the preceding books. For every studious and diligent reader (with the help of God) will be able to easily understand and find in them all other secrets and mysteries hidden and covered there, which are beyond comparison greater and more difficult than in this one. Through this one I have provided the subject with equally ample cause: so much so that whoever wishes to use it with prudence will easily be able, by their own wit, to surpass our own. And if anyone desires this path [to be] more beautiful in its shadow <note>The "shadow" refers to the deceptive outer layer of the cipher—the text that hides the secret message.</note>, they must employ their spirit along with their senses, hands, and brain: and they themselves must prepare and dispose themselves to create (if they wish) a more beautiful way through more appropriate and elegant paraphrases and dictions. And notably, and above all, whoever takes pleasure in and wishes to use this present form of occult writing <term>occult writing: cryptography or secret writing intended to be hidden from the uninitiated</term>, must be mindful and remember to always remain within its destined and prefixed circle and order: which, if exceeded or failed in any way (however small it may be), renders the work completely deficient <note>Trithemius warns that the slightest error in following the sequence of the tables will make the entire encrypted message impossible to decode.</note>.

<vocab>Polygraphy, third book, occult writing, paraphrases, secrets, mysteries</vocab>

<summary>Johannes Trithemius concludes the third book of his work, encouraging readers to use his cryptographic system as a foundation to create their own elegant and sophisticated secret messages. He emphasizes that the system requires absolute precision, as even a minor mistake in following the established order will break the code.</summary>
<keywords>cryptography, epilogue, occult writing, Johannes Trithemius, paraphrasing, coding errors, secret mysteries</keywords>

<header>THIRD BOOK</header>

truncated, and of no value. And to this effect we have found, and can find, several names of men and infinite words <term>vocables: individual words or terms used as building blocks for a code</term> of cities, towns, villages, countries, islands, rivers, woods, trees, herbs, flowers, roots, colors, stones, and other innumerable similar things, which can properly serve and be adapted to this our instruction and book. By the contents of which, and the understanding of what is included therein, one will be able to judge how easily other books can be made using other different means and styles, which would be beyond comparison more excellent, singular, and elegant than ours: provided that with good and due diligence the mind is prompt and quick. But for one who cannot understand this so easy, indeed more than childish, subject: how will he penetrate or understand what has been said before, and what remains still to be said, which is beyond comparison much more subtle and difficult? Now, desiring to make no further account of this, both because of the great ease found therein, and also to avoid being tiresome <note>original: "envieux par prolixité" — in this context, the author wishes to avoid being tedious or causing "annoyance" to the reader by being overly wordy about simple matters.</note> through wordiness, I

# First expanded figure of the
## DIRECT TABLE <note>Original: "TABLE RECTE". In early cryptography, a "direct table" refers to a grid where the alphabets shift forward in standard alphabetical order, rather than backward or in a scrambled sequence.</note>.

<note>In the table below, the first letter of each pair is printed in red ink in the original manuscript.</note>

| | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **a** b | **a** c | **a** d | **a** e | **a** f |
| **b** c | **b** d | **b** e | **b** f | **b** g |
| **c** d | **c** e | **c** f | **c** g | **c** h |
| **d** e | **d** f | **d** g | **d** h | **d** i |
| **e** f | **e** g | **e** h | **e** i | **e** k |
| **f** g | **f** h | **f** i | **f** k | **f** l |
| **g** h | **g** i | **g** k | **g** l | **g** m |
| **h** i | **h** k | **h** l | **h** m | **h** n |
| **i** k | **i** l | **i** m | **i** n | **i** o |
| **k** l | **k** m | **k** n | **k** o | **k** p |
| **l** m | **l** n | **l** o | **l** p | **l** q |
| **m** n | **m** o | **m** p | **m** q | **m** r |
| **n** o | **n** p | **n** q | **n** r | **n** s |
| **o** p | **o** q | **o** r | **o** s | **o** t |
| **p** q | **p** r | **p** s | **p** t | **p** u |
| **q** r | **q** s | **q** t | **q** u | **q** x |
| **r** s | **r** t | **r** u | **r** x | **r** y |
| **s** t | **s** u | **s** x | **s** y | **s** z |
| **t** u | **t** x | **t** y | **t** z | **t** & |
| **u** x | **u** y | **u** z | **u** & | **u** a |
| **x** y | **x** z | **x** & | **x** a | **x** b |
| **y** z | **y** & | **y** a | **y** b | **y** c |
| **z** & | **z** a | **z** b | **z** c | **z** d |
| **&** a | **&** b | **&** c | **&** d | **&** e |

This is the first figure of expansion and dilation <note>A mathematical or logical stretching of the basic cipher table.</note> of the first canonical and direct table, where five alphabets are described by metathesis <note>Original: "metathese", meaning the transposition or swapping of letters.</note> and transposition. In the first alphabet of this figure, 'b' is taken and used for 'a'; 'c' for 'b'; and so on, as clearly appears to any observer. In the second alphabet, 'c' is taken and used for 'a'; 'd' for 'b', etc. In the third, 'd' represents and is worth 'a'; 'e', for 'b'; 'f', for 'c'. In the fourth, 'e' for 'a'; 'f' for 'b'. In the fifth, 'f' for 'a'. The whole is as the arrangement of the order of letters shows and manifests in this first figure.

<term>polygraphy</term>: cryptography; the study of multiple ways of writing.
<term>direct table</term>: an alphabetical grid where shifts move in forward sequence.
<term>metathesis</term>: the transposition of letters.
<term>transposition</term>: shifting letters to different positions.
<term>alphabet</term>: here, a specific substitute sequence.
<term>canonical</term>: standard or fundamental.
<term>dilation</term>: the expansion of a simple rule into a larger table.

<summary>This page presents an "expanded" cryptographic table showing five different alphabet shifts used for substitution, explaining how each column represents a new cipher key. It demonstrates the transition from a simple substitution to a polyalphabetic system where one letter can be represented by multiple substitutes.</summary>
<keywords>cryptography, polyalphabetic cipher, Tabula Recta, transposition, Johannes Trithemius, substitution table, metathesis</keywords>

### DIRECT TABLE. <note>Original: "TABLE RECTE". This refers to a standard cryptographic grid where the alphabet shifts forward by a set number of positions.</note>

In this second expanded figure of the first direct and canonical table, I have similarly described and arranged five orders of alphabets: from which, and by means of these, you will be able to create several others, by <term>metathesis</term> <note>The transposition or swapping of letters or sounds within a word</note>, transposition, or <term>orcheme</term> <note>Original Greek-derived term meaning "dance"; in this context, it refers to the rhythmic or patterned movement of letters through the table</note>, if it seems good to you. And for your understanding, I have extracted the following example from the first row and column of this present figure: n g h z p l r k l i u r g t n l k l a u b z &.

# Third expanded figure of the
## DIRECT TABLE. <note>Original: "TABLE RECTE." A "direct" or "right" table is a cryptographic grid where the alphabet shifts by a consistent increment, as opposed to a reversed or "transverse" table.</note>

| | | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| a m | a n | a o | a p | a q |
| b n | b o | b p | b q | b r |

| f r | f s | f t | f u | f x |

| i u | i x | i y | i z | i & |
| k x | k y | k z | k & | k a |
| l y | l z | l & | l a | l b |
| m z | m & | m a | m b | m c |
| n & | n a | n b | n c | n d |
| o a | o b | o c | o d | o e |
| p b | p c | p d | p e | p f |
| q c | q d | q e | q f | q g |
| r d | r e | r f | r g | r h |

| t f | t g | t h | t i | t k |
| u g | u h | u i | u k | u l |
| x h | x i | x k | x l | x m |
| y i | y k | y l | y m | y n |
| z k | z l | z m | z n | z o |
| & l | & m | & n | & o | & p |

You will also find in this third expanded figure of the first direct and canonical <note>original: "canonique". Refers to the standard or fundamental rule for the cipher.</note> table, five alphabets, distributed and arranged in five rows and columns: in the first of which (as you see), by reason of <term>metathesis</term> <note>metathesis: the transposition or switching of the positions of letters</note> and transposition, **m** is taken for **a**; in the second, **n** for **a**; in the third, **o** for **a**; in the fourth, **p** for **a**; and in the fifth, **q** for **a**. And the number and quantity of these can thus be expanded through metathesis in innumerable and almost infinite ways, as has been stated.

This is the fourth expanded <term>metathetical</term> <note>metathetical: relating to metathesis, the transposition or switching of the positions of letters.</note> and transpositional figure of the aforementioned first direct table; which, being composed of five alphabets like the preceding ones, includes within itself up to the twentieth alphabet. <note>Since each "expanded figure" in this book contains 5 alphabet shifts, the fourth figure concludes the 20th shift of the system.</note> And by the same means, through this figure you will be able to perform (as has been stated before) great and nearly innumerable transpositions, which will serve you surely and secretly in your mystical affairs <note>Original: "affaires myſtiques." In Renaissance cryptography, "mystical" often referred to "hidden" or "occult" communications—those intended to be kept secret from the uninitiated.</note>, whenever it pleases you to use them.

# Fifth expanded figure of the
## DIRECT TABLE. <note>The "Direct Table" is the primary cryptographic grid where letters are shifted in a standard, sequential order.</note>

| | | | | |
|----------|----------|----------|----------|----------|
| **a** y | **a** z | **a** & | **a** c | **a** g |
| **b** z | **b** & | **b** a | **b** e | **b** i |
| **c** & | **c** a | **c** b | **c** g | **c** l |
| **d** a | **d** b | **d** c | **d** i | **d** n |
| **e** b | **e** c | **e** d | **e** l | **e** p |
| **f** c | **f** d | **f** e | **f** n | **f** r |
| **g** d | **g** e | **g** f | **g** p | **g** t |
| **h** e | **h** f | **h** g | **h** r | **h** x |
| **i** f | **i** g | **i** h | **i** t | **i** z |
| **k** g | **k** h | **k** i | **k** x | **k** & |
| **l** h | **l** i | **l** k | **l** z | **l** b |
| **m** i | **m** k | **m** l | **m** & | **m** d |
| **n** k | **n** l | **m** m | **n** b | **n** f |
| **o** l | **o** m | **o** n | **o** d | **o** h |
| **p** m | **p** n | **p** o | **p** f | **p** k |
| **q** n | **q** o | **q** p | **q** h | **q** m |
| **r** o | **r** p | **r** q | **r** k | **r** o |
| **s** p | **s** q | **s** r | **s** m | **s** q |
| **t** q | **t** r | **t** s | **t** o | **t** s |
| **u** r | **u** s | **u** t | **u** q | **u** u |
| **x** s | **x** t | **x** u | **x** s | **x** y |
| **y** t | **y** u | **y** x | **y** u | **y** a |
| **z** u | **z** x | **z** y | **z** y | **z** c |
| **&** x | **&** y | **&** z | **&** a | **&** e |

This is the fifth and last expanded figure of the aforementioned first direct table, containing within itself (as far as it concerns the said first table) only three alphabets, to satisfy and complete the number of twenty-three. And if you add the usual and common alphabet, it would return to twenty-four, following the number of the <term>alphabetics</term> <note>Letters of the alphabet.</note>. And the other two orders or columns, being there beyond the twenty-four, relate and refer to the <term>orcheme</term> <note>Original: 'orcheme'. Derived from the Greek word for dance, here it refers to a rhythmic "leap" or patterned skip in the progression of the letters.</note> and leap of a letter or note to its third following letter, and always by threes. Now, I have wished to describe these last two columns here only to serve as an example, and to show how to make a more ample and great <term>ampliation</term> <note>Expansion or enlargement of the system.</note>, there and when the <term>operator</term> <note>The person encoding the message.</note> desires.

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

# First expanded figure of the
## **REVERSE TABLE**. <note>The "Reverse Table" (Table Averse) is a cryptographic tool where the substitution alphabet runs in the opposite direction of the standard alphabet, creating a mirrored effect.</note>

| | | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **a** & | **a** z | **a** y | **a** x | **a** u |
| **b** z | **b** y | **b** x | **b** u | **b** t |
| **c** y | **c** x | **c** u | **c** t | **c** s |
| **d** x | **d** u | **d** t | **d** s | **d** r |
| **e** u | **e** t | **e** s | **e** r | **e** q |
| **f** t | **f** s | **f** r | **f** q | **f** p |
| **g** s | **g** r | **g** q | **g** p | **g** o |
| **h** r | **h** q | **h** p | **h** o | **h** n |
| **i** q | **i** p | **i** o | **i** n | **i** m |
| **k** p | **k** o | **k** n | **k** m | **k** l |
| **l** o | **l** n | **l** m | **l** l | **l** k |
| **m** n | **m** m | **m** l | **m** k | **m** i |
| **n** m | **n** l | **n** k | **n** i | **n** h |
| **o** l | **o** k | **o** i | **o** h | **o** g |
| **p** k | **p** i | **p** h | **p** g | **p** f |
| **q** i | **q** h | **q** g | **q** f | **q** e |
| **r** h | **r** g | **r** f | **r** e | **r** d |
| **s** g | **s** f | **s** e | **s** d | **s** c |
| **t** f | **t** e | **t** d | **t** c | **t** b |
| **u** e | **u** d | **u** c | **u** b | **u** a |
| **x** d | **x** c | **x** b | **x** a | **x** & |
| **y** c | **y** b | **y** a | **y** & | **y** z |
| **z** b | **z** a | **z** & | **z** z | **z** y |
| **&** a | **&** & | **&** z | **&** y | **&** x |

After having described the preceding figures of the direct table, I wished consequently to place and set down here the first expanded figure of the reverse table. This one I can, with good and just cause, describe and call "irregular." Insofar as I have changed the alphabets within it alternately according to the order and norm, one finds many faults and errors therein, due to the <term>literal eclipses and conjunctions</term> <note>These terms refer to mathematical overlaps or gaps in the sequence where letters repeat or are skipped unexpectedly due to the logic of the cipher grid.</note> that occur there—even in this first figure of expansion, after the twelfth letter backward. For **m** does not vary, nor does the character **&**, in the second column. Likewise, **l** and **z** are eclipsed in the fourth row. I have not wished to change or correct this, seeing that this error proceeds from the norm and rule of the reverse table itself, as it rises in reverse and against the direct table.

The author chooses to preserve these flaws as they are a natural consequence of the reverse-shifting logic.</summary>

In this second expanded figure of the reverse table, you will find six alphabets: in the first of which, **k** & **y**; in the third, **i** & **x**; in the fifth, **h** & **u**, never change or vary. This seems to me to be of little importance, since the standard and the rule mandate and require it so. Additionally, it would be difficult, indeed impossible, to find a man in the world (no matter how expert he might be) who could notice the constancy, <term>gemination</term> <note>From the Latin "geminare," meaning the doubling or pairing of characters.</note>, and duplication of one or two single characters, given the great and almost infinite number of variations that can be made according to what is contained in these tables and this book.

The author notes that certain characters remain fixed in specific columns but argues that this does not compromise security due to the vast number of possible variations.</summary>

<header>FOURTH BOOK</header>

# Third expanded figure of the
## REVERSE TABLE.

This third expanded figure of the <term>reverse table<note>A cryptographic system where the cipher alphabet is written in reverse order relative to the plain text alphabet.</note></term>, in its nature and form, contains nothing new except for the <term>metathesis<note>original: "metathese"; the transposition or shifting of letters within the grid.</note></term> that is common to all the other preceding and following figures, extending to infinite degrees and numbers. Now, there are six <term>transposed alphabets<note>original: "alphabets transposez"; columns where the alphabet has been shifted to create different substitution keys.</note></term>, in the first of which **t** and **g** are <term>eclipsed<note>original: "eclypsez"; instances where letters overlap or are skipped due to the mathematical progression of the table.</note></term> and joined; in the third, **s** and **f**; in the fifth, **r** and **e**. And the inevitable cause of these eclipses is clearly demonstrated by the rules, sequence, and alphabetic standards.

There may be several faults and errors found in this fourth expanded figure of the said <term>reverse table<note>A cryptographic table where the cipher alphabet is mapped against the plain text in reverse order.</note></term>, according to the <term>canonical calculation<note>original: "supputation canoniale"; refers to the formal mathematical or rule-based method used to generate these sequences.</note></term>. Now, in the first alphabet q and d, in the third c and p, and in the fifth, o and b, are neither moved nor changed, but rather conjoined and <term>eclipsed<note>original: "eclypsez"; a cryptographic term used here to describe letters that are merged or omitted in the shifting sequence.</note></term>.

Following this <term>orchemale</term><note>Meaning "pertaining to transition or leaping."</note> or transition figure, one can understand the form and manner—through transposition and leaping—of creating an infinity of alphabets, as much by the standard rule of order as by the positioning of the alphabetical letters. Now, the aforementioned six orchemale columns will suffice to serve as an example for those who might not be content or satisfied with the alphabets included and arranged here: so that by means of these, they will easily be able to obtain the form and manner (as has been said) to invent and create an infinity of other completely different ones, which they will do easily without number, indeed without end, if they so wish.

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

## To the Reader.

<image-desc>An elaborate historiated woodcut initial 'J' featuring several figures in a classical or academic setting, including a seated figure and a child, surrounded by ornate foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>
I HAVE FOUND and find it marvelously strange that the ancient and first Latins, and those who formerly ordered and arranged our Latin and common letters, did not make them numerical, nor make them subject to the logic and order of numbers and calculations: as the Greeks and also the Hebrews knew well how to do, and still do; who, through the doubling and duplication of certain of their letters, have established signs and characters up to the quantity of twenty-eight, which can easily serve for all numbers and calculations in the world. The Greeks also, by similar curiosity and foresight, increased the deficiency of their alphabetical letters by the addition and expansion of four other characters. We, then, having the number of twenty-four letters—counting and including this character '&' <note>The ampersand was historically treated as the 24th letter of the alphabet</note>—why should we not make them numerical and subject to the logic of number, seeing that we can just as easily invent and admit four more doubled and paired characters? Of these I provide an example hereafter, which seems to me sufficient to serve every number, making a <term>m</term> and a <term>final m</term>; an <term>r</term> and a <term>rotunda r</term> <note>original: Ʀ, a variant of the letter 'r' used after rounded letters</note>; a <term>long s</term> <note>original: ſ, the tall version of 's' used at the start or middle of words</note> and a <term>final</term> or <term>closed s</term>; and also a <term>closed u</term> and an <term>open v</term>. By adding and assembling these four aforementioned characters with our twenty-four common and usual alphabetical letters, we will have by this means twenty-eight letters and characters, which will universally suffice for all numbers. And to learn and understand this form and manner of

<header>ON POLYGRAPHY. VI</header>

<meta>Visible bleed-through of a table from the following page (verso).</meta>

To calculate, count, and number will require little effort, and even less ingenuity, for those who (however slightly) have knowledge of the letters of the alphabet, once they have understood it and fixed it in their memory but a single time. And I believe that this invention of ours can be greatly useful and profitable to them when they wish to use and employ it; for in a few letters they will encompass many thousands in number. All these things stated here before and hereafter (to this effect) can easily be understood, known, and discerned at first glance and without any calculation, clearer than the light of day. Although many, not practiced or experienced in the <term>art of calculation</term> and arithmetic, will find it difficult for this to be done using <term>Arabic numerals</term> <note>original: "figures d’algarithme," referring to the decimal system using the digits 0-9, which was still being popularized over Roman numerals</note>, especially with large numbers; for as soon as you have seen a number, however large it may be, you will be able to fully understand and express it without circumlocution, division, or separation of words. Now I have specifically wished to record and set down here the numerical letters, arranged and organized to represent numbers, so that this following order and table may serve as an example for you; and that

->by it you may see with your own eyes,<-
->how this invention will be found<-
->no less useful and profitable,<-
->than easy and simple to<-
->understand.<-

By the above-described method of numbering and counting in Latin and common letters, every intelligent reader who wishes to make use of it should (it seems to me) be content and satisfied with what we have said and written here. This is especially true given that one can easily—more than easily—extend, amplify, and expand this system as much as they wish, even unto infinite numbers, and do so with very few letters. Furthermore, those who are pleased by this and take interest in this numerical mode and method of <term>supputation</term> <note>An archaic term for calculation or mathematical reckoning.</note> will afterwards be able to easily follow and understand the mode and manner of numbers and calculation used by the ancients. To ensure that those less familiar may more easily understand it, it will not be troublesome or tedious for me (though I already feel weary from the labor) to provide and describe here, through the arrangement and order of the following characters and letters, the form and method which Hunibald the historiographer <note>A semi-legendary chronicler often cited in early modern texts as a primary source for Frankish history.</note>, Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (672–735), an English monk famous for his chronological works.</note>, Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Carolingian scholar who wrote extensively on the "computus," or the calculation of dates.</note>, Helperic <note>Helperic of Auxerre, a 9th-century monk known for his influential textbook on the ecclesiastical calendar.</note>, and several other ancients have used. They employed these specifically in their descriptions of chronicles and their ecclesiastical calculations and reckonings, using the numerical order, phrasing, and style that follow.

## Ancient Order of the Numerical Letters.

I have until now detailed and described, by way of example, the manner and method of writing numbers and the numerical systems of the Ancients using Latin and common letters; this was done so that those unfamiliar with them might understand them more easily. As for the fact that in the preceding description and arrangement of the Arabic numerals <term>figures d'algorithme; the ten digits (0-9) used in modern calculation as opposed to Roman numerals</term>, I may have in some places departed from the strict order and rules of true calculation <term>supputation; the formal mathematical process of counting or computation</term> and the form of counting, this was not due to error, nor through fault or omission. Rather, I decided to do so for good and sensible reasons: specifically, so that I would not weary myself or my readers with too great a progression or lengthiness. In the following illustration, transcribed shortly hereafter, readers will see other numerical methods and orders through which the ancients expressed their largest numbers.

# Alphabetic order and mode of writing of the ancient Northerners and Normans.

All letters and all characters, whether Greek or Palestinian <note>original: "Palestins," likely referring to Hebrew or Phoenician scripts as they were understood in the 16th century</note>, are subject to the logic of number and calculation <note>original: "supputation," meaning mathematical computation</note>: as we have already said several times before. However, in our Latin alphabet which we use, we have only seven numeral letters subject to the logic of number: namely, **c, d, i, l, m, v,** and **x**. <note>These represent the Roman numerals 100, 500, 1, 50, 1000, 5, and 10.</note> But the Normans <term>Nortmants: Here referring to Northern European peoples, including Vikings</term>, along with the Dacians <note>original: "Daces," likely referring to the Danes, as Renaissance authors often conflated Dacia (in modern Romania) with Denmark</note>, descended from the Asiatic and Scandinavian islands, when they were making war against the Gauls, wishing to provide for the secrecy and security of their counsel (following what Bede <term>Beda: Saint Bede the Venerable (c. 672–735), an English monk and scholar</term>, a monk in England, writes of it), extracted and borrowed from the Greek alphabet a new and unique method of writing. They adapted and very well conformed the Greek numbers (including the ten) to the twenty-four Latin letters and characters that we use today. And by this means, under the scheme and pretext of another and foreign system, they knew very well how to cover and hide the order of our letters and characters which we are accustomed to using: writing for **a**, 1; for **b**, 2; for **c**, 3; for **d**, 4; and so on consecutively, until the end of our usual alphabet. And it seems to me that this invention and form of writing is quite beautiful and secure, and that it could not be understood by a Greek or Latin man without great difficulty. For here the total and entire [Greek] alphabet is not found, but only nine letters of it, along with this letter or numeral mark, **Ϛ** <note>original: "stigma," a Greek ligature used to represent the number 6</note>, which signifies six. And for this reason, it is set and placed in the rank and order of **f**, which is the sixth letter in our Latin alphabet.

Furthermore, we have also added for the twenty-fourth letter this character, **&**, to serve as an abbreviation in our common tongue, wishing in this to follow and imitate the Greeks. Now, by the means and management of this above-written alphabet, the Northerners and Normans <term>Nortmans: Here used broadly for North Sea peoples or Scandinavians</term> wrote securely and secretly the whole conception of their wishes; and this they did without any suspicion or doubt of being discovered or understood by Latins or Greeks, even though all the characters used are Greek, representing however by their numerical order our Latin letters, as has been said.

One will easily be able to change and vary this alphabet in several ways, seeing that by changing the number through transposition <term>metathese: the rearrangement of letters or components</term> and composition, the character also, and the letter, are varied and changed. Any studious person who understands this secret will be able, easily and at their will, to arrange and do this with the same solid and fixed letters of the Greeks. It further seems to me that the form and composition of these bodies of letters will not be found too deformed or difficult, especially to those who have practiced and used them even a little.

They are also (in my judgment) quite suitable and proper for the description of our common and ordinary French language, as we are able through them to write and give a universal understanding of all things that may present themselves, and in all languages which are or may be known to us. And it must be noted that whenever the character **iota** <note>original: "iota," the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet (ι)</note> is placed by itself, it signifies the letter **k**, which is the tenth letter of our alphabet; and where it must signify **i**, it must be punctuated and have a point placed above it, as is marked here, to show the

CHARLEMAGNE, the Most Christian King and Emperor, having for a long time (and for nearly the space of thirty years) fought and made war against the **Saxons**, and having defeated and subjugated them to his empire and domination by force of arms: constrained and submitted them to the Christian faith, law, and religion. And fearing that they might once again apostatize <note>To "apostatize" means to renounce one's religious faith, a major concern for Charlemagne after forced conversions.</note> and fall away from the faith—as they had already done several times—he established several scouts, to whom he ordained the office of **Judicature** <note>This refers to a judicial body or system of judges.</note>. He commanded and enjoined them most expressly that, as they traveled and marched throughout all that country and land, they should inquire secretly and diligently into the form, manner, and way of life of every person. 

He further ordered that all those found by them—no matter how minor their status—who were apostates or falling away from the faith, thieves, blasphemers, or those speaking ill of the Church or its priests and ministers, or those treating ecclesiastical commands and rules with contempt: or those who by word, sign, subornation, secret meeting, conspiracy <note>original: "monopole." In this era, it refers to an illegal gathering or a plot rather than a commercial monopoly.</note>, or otherwise had troubled (or should trouble in any way whatsoever) the order, policy, and statutes of the religion and the **Christian Commonwealth**, aspiring and wishing to reduce, seduce, and suborn the people to **Paganism**: should immediately, without delay or postponement, by his Royal and Imperial authority, be hanged and strangled, or put to death by whatever fashion or other means possible. 

And to the end that his ordinances and institution should remain perpetually inviolate and untainted, he granted to the aforementioned delegates total power and authority to substitute and appoint others in their place, under certain conditions and provided they were sufficient and capable. These men, using the same power, might, and authority, and exercising their state and office of **Inquisition**, would have the power to put to death all those attained and convicted of the aforementioned contraventions. 

And he likewise sent them secret laws and ordinances, written in the aforementioned **characters** <note>The secret alphabets or ciphers discussed in previous chapters.</note>, or others unknown to all the world except themselves: ordaining and describing point by point the form and manner that his majesty wished and intended for them to use in their office, in order to proceed justly to condemnation or punishment; to the end that by this means good judgment and good justice might be inviolably and secretly maintained and observed. And for this effect, they used in those times several other unknown alphabets and characters, which at present are unknown and lost to us, as much because of the length of time as for...

Any person who desires, or wishes to create and arrange according to their pleasure alphabets composed of new characters, must necessarily observe the three following points, which seem to me to have been poorly observed in the preceding alphabets. The first is that it is necessary to form the characters well, and with the smoothest and easiest stroke and body possible; the more simple and easy they are, the better they will be judged. The second is that it is needful and necessary to make the characters of such measure, proportion, and arrangement that, when they are joined and assembled together, they can form an orderly flow with a good style of writing, and as little deformity as possible. And for the third point, one must consider making <term>double letters</term> <note>Likely referring to "final" forms of letters (like those in Hebrew) or specific ligatures used to vary the appearance of the code.</note> like the Hebrews, so that by this means the writing may be more secret and unknown.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was Rome's most famous orator. He is credited with the invention of the first Roman shorthand system, known as Tironian Notes, through his secretary Tiro.</note> the eloquent orator of the Romans, had written and produced a book no less great than it was laborious and difficult, full of notes and characters: which later Saint Cyprian the Martyr <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 CE). ## METHOD AND MEANS,
### by which one can safely and secretly communicate all secrets, as much by numbers as by usual and common letters.

<image-desc>Large decorative historiated initial 'I' depicting three human figures in a landscape within an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc> I do not wish to deny, but rather freely confess, that all the things previously said by me, or that I might say hereafter (concerning <term>private and foreign characters and alphabets</term> <note>The author is referring to "peregrine" or exotic alphabets, often invented or borrowed from ancient sources to hide text.</note>), are childish, frivolous, and of little consequence: considering that anyone at their pleasure and will could devise and form an infinity of others, incomparably more beautiful than those which have been described by us in this book. Any person, understanding this present figure and <term>Orchemal</term> <note>From the Greek word for "dance," used here to describe the rhythmic, shifting nature of the letters and numbers in the table.</note> table, will be able, by means of it, to draw, extract, and compose as many and as great a number of alphabets as they wish and please. And for an easier understanding of it, I have placed and set at the four corners and squares the alphabetical letters of the Latins, facing and opposing one another: so that by this means and by this <term>Orcheme</term> and leap, every operator can, through transpositions, create an infinity of alphabets. However, there is a need here for subtlety and diligence, along with a good memory: so that due to the great quantity and multitude of numbers, the operator’s understanding and memory are not confounded.

I have for good reason, and not without cause, decided not to expand or stretch out the aforementioned <term>anomalous table</term> <note>A cipher table where the relationships between letters and numbers do not follow a simple, predictable sequence, making it harder to crack.</note> at length: specifically because of the great and extreme pains and mental labor that would be required for the progression and expansion necessary for its full extension, which would be an infinite task. An elaborate woodcut border frames the central title text. At the top center is the French royal coat of arms featuring three fleurs-de-lis, surmounted by a crown and flanked by garlands of fruit and two globes—one terrestrial and one celestial. The side borders are composed of various mathematical, navigational, and astronomical instruments, including armillary spheres, compasses, quadrants, rulers, a plumb bob, and an hourglass. 

At the bottom corners, two unicorns (the printer's mark for Jacques Kerver) sit on grassy mounds holding shields; the shield on the left contains a printer's mark featuring a cross and a monogram. In the bottom center, a winged head (representing Genius or Wit) is chained to a heavy rectangular stone block labeled "PENIA" (Poverty). Two scrolls flanking the chain read "VOLATVM" and "TOLLIT" (forming the phrase "Penia volatvm tollit" — Poverty hinders the flight of genius). Below this entire scene is a ribbon with the anagrammatic motto "L'ANGE REGAL DOCIBLE".

**Archimedes of Syracuse** <note>A famous Greek mathematician and inventor (c. 287–212 BC). While the author attributes this device to him, this "stick" method is more famously known as the "Scytale," used by the ancient Spartans for military encryption</note>, prince of mathematicians, would have two sticks planed and fashioned into round, square, or triangular shapes, of the same length, width, and thickness. Afterward, he would keep one for himself and give or send the other to his absent friend. Whenever one wished to write secretly to the other, he would prepare a <term>schedule</term> <note>original: "schedule"; a term for a small strip or scroll of parchment or paper</note>, or rather a <term>strip</term> <note>original: "tringle"</note> of white paper, of narrow width and twice the length of one of the sticks. After wrapping the stick with the strip or schedule of paper and attaching the two ends with wax to the top and bottom of the stick, he would write upon the said strip. He ensured that each letter or character fell across the cuts and seams of the paper where it was duly joined together. Once this was done, he would remove the paper from the stick, and suddenly there appeared such a great distance and separation between the letters that no letter or word followed or connected with another at all. # ON POLYGRAPHY <note>original: "DE POLYGRAPHIE"; from the Greek words for "many" and "writing," referring here to the study of various secret scripts and ciphers.</note>

This writing cannot be seen, or known in any way, except by those who are informed of the secret, and through the use and employment of **powders, waters, washes, fires, fumigations** <note>the process of exposing a surface to smoke or vapors to reveal hidden ink</note>, and other things necessary and required for this science and form of **Dermatic** letters <note>derived from the Greek *derma*, meaning skin; writing intended to be hidden on the human body</note>.

The second kind of invisible characters is called **Hyphasmatic** <note>derived from the Greek *hyphasma*, meaning a woven garment or fabric</note>: by which one can write on cloths, linens, fabrics, or clothing, using certain liniments, inks, pigments <note>original: "encostes"; refers to coloring matter or thick inks</note>, or washes, which, being dry and dried, cannot be seen or known at all. However, when they are soaked and wetted in very cold water, they are seen, known, and read easily; otherwise, they could not appear. For this reason, it has been called **Hyphalmic** <note>likely referring to the use of salt or brine (Greek *halme*), or perhaps a variation of the term for fabric-writing</note>, or **Hyphasmatic**.

The third kind of invisible characters is called **Alleotic** <note>from the Greek *alloios*, meaning "of a different kind" or "to change"; referring to writing that changes state to become visible</note>: and it is done in several ways, as much by form as by material. Through this kind, one can find infinite and innumerable means to write occultly and secretly. First, I describe and mark the leap of the letters, extensively and at length; which I afterwards reduce into an <term>Orcheme|original: Orcheme. And for this purpose I have doubled and <term>geminated|From the Latin 'geminare,' meaning to double or pair. We then, being in the same necessity and shortage of letters and notes, why shall we not seek the means to amplify them, to make them numerical and subject to numerical logic, admitting and introducing with our common and usual letters these two notes, that is to say this character, &, which commonly and for abbreviation we put for "and"? <note>The author refers to the ampersand, which originated as a ligature of the letters 'e' and 't' (the Latin word 'et,' meaning 'and').</note> And it matters not for the understanding and form of cipher or numerical writing whether it is written thus, &: or indeed, in full, "and": provided that in its rank, order, and number, it represents six.

### THE WORK AND LITTLE KEY <note>original: "L'OEVVRE ET CLAVICVLE"; "Clavicule" (from the Latin 'clavicula') literally means "little key," a term traditionally used for technical manuals on secrets or ciphers.</note>

# THE WORK AND KEY.

Therefore, to pursue our subject and the interpretation of the obscurities that may be, or seem to be, in this work of **Polygraphy** <term>Polygraphy: A term popularized by Johannes Trithemius referring to complex cryptography and universal writing systems.</term>, our author says there are three species of secret writing.

The first of these is called **Dermatic**, which was once widely known and common among soldiers. **Pliny** (it seems to me) in his twenty-eighth book, describes another sort of it, calling it **Tithymallus** <note>original: "Tythimale"; referring to the genus *Euphorbia*.</note>, which is (he says) in common language, "milk-weed"; others call it "goat’s lettuce," and in our French language, **Spurge** <note>original: "Eſpurge"</note>. It is said that if one writes with the "milk" <note>The white, latex-like sap of the spurge plant.</note> of this herb on any surface, the writing cannot be read unless the paper, or whatever else has been written upon, is first burned. Then, by sprinkling a little clear water upon the ash, the letters and writing will easily appear.

And it is found in writing that in ancient times, adulterers and unfaithful women found this method the most secret of all occult writings, preferring to use it far more than any other.
