A large circular cryptographic diagram or <term>volvelle: a rotating paper instrument used in early books to perform calculations or decodings</term> divided into twenty-four radial sectors. At the top center (12 o'clock position) is a small box containing a cross symbol. Moving clockwise from the top, the sectors are indexed with red lowercase letters **a** through **m** (though some are partially obscured). Moving counter-clockwise from the top, the sectors are indexed with red letters **z** through **n**.

Each sector contains a vertical column of characters. The sector labeled with the red letter **a** contains the standard Latin alphabet letters: **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m**. The sector labeled with the red letter **z** contains the letters: **n, o, p, q, r, s, t, u, x, y, z**. The remaining sectors contain various non-standard, alchemical, or invented cipher characters.

In the center of the wheel is a circular medallion featuring a face (possibly a sun or a lion) with radiating lines. On the right side of the page, a large, ornate decorative paper overlay or <term>cartouche: an ornamental frame, often resembling a scroll, used to highlight specific information</term> with strapwork and floral patterns covers a portion of the diagram. This overlay contains two vertical scales of red numbers: the top scale runs from 1 to 12 in ascending order, and the bottom scale runs from 12 to 1 in descending order. The four corners of the page are decorated with leafy garlands.

# Enneagrammaton. <note>From the Greek *ennea* (nine) and *gramma* (letter/line), referring to a nine-part grid system.</note>

<image-desc>A cryptographic diagram illustrating the "Enneagrammaton" or Pigpen cipher. It consists of a 3x3 grid formed by double horizontal and vertical lines. Within each of the nine cells, characters are written in red ink, with sets of dots (one, two, or three) positioned beneath them to indicate their order within the cell. The shape of the grid lines around a cell, combined with the number of dots, forms the cipher character.
- Top row cells: [a b c], [d e f], [g h i]
- Middle row cells: [k l m], [n o p], [q r s]
- Bottom row cells: [t u x], [y z &], [2 more d p l]
The last cell indicates "2 de plus" (two more) to complete the set of symbols.</image-desc>

# ARTS OF DESIGN

<note>The title "Arts of Design" is printed around the perimeter of a circular emblem. This emblem is set into a green textured leather cover, which is finished with a delicate gold-tooled border along the top edge.</note>

<term>Arts of Design<note>During this period, the "Arts of Design" (derived from the Italian *disegno*) typically referred to the foundational disciplines of painting, sculpture, and architecture, all of which were believed to be united by the essential skill of drawing.</note></term>

<term>Monogram<note>In the center of the cover's label is an interlaced monogram of the letters **H**, **K**, and **R**. Such markings often indicate the owner of the book, the artist, or a specific institution.</note></term>

<term>Bookbinding<note>The green leather and gold tooling suggest a high-quality, professional binding, intended to protect and elevate the status of the manuscript within a library.</note></term>

->**STRONGLY AND GENTLY**<-
<note>original: "FORTITER ET SVAVITER"</note>

<term>Strongly and Gently<note>A translation of the Latin motto "Fortiter et Svaviter." This phrase was historically used by various noble families and religious orders, such as the Jesuits, to express a philosophy of being firm in principle and action, yet mild and gracious in manner.</note></term>

<term>Monogram<note>The central decorative element consists of the interlaced letters **S** and **M**. In the context of book collecting, such monograms usually denote the initials of the book’s owner or the person who commissioned the binding.</note></term>

<term>Heraldry<note>The emblem follows the conventions of heraldic design, featuring a central shield-like oval surrounded by scrolling ornamentation. This style was often used to create a "supra-libros," a mark of ownership stamped onto the outside of a book.</note></term>

<term>Binding<note>The use of dark red leather with embossed decoration signifies a high-status object. Such bindings were intended not only to protect the pages but to serve as a decorative element in a scholar's or aristocrat's library.</note></term>
